_deprecated.note: shipsTransiting, stranded, throughputPercent, transitsBaseline, insuranceMultiple, and status mix sources or are scalar projections of richer objects. status in particular switches producer (PortWatch, falling back to AIS) without saying which; use transits.*, insurance.*, dailyTransits.*, and verdict.status instead.

aisBaselineNote: transitsBaseline is withheld (null) until 72 hourly samples exist on the current tiled12-active30m-fix60 basis. The basis last reset on 2026-09-26, when vessels whose last AIS fix is an hour or more old stopped counting as holding position or moving; before that it reset on 2026-07-30 (tiling, counts up roughly 3.4x) and 2026-07-20 (30-minute window). After each reset the median is withheld for about 3 days while samples on the new basis build up. Samples on an earlier basis are not mixed in. It is an AIS concurrent-presence median, a different population from transits.baseline (IMF PortWatch daily crossings); do not divide one by the other.
aisFirstFixNote: aisConcurrentInZone counts only vessels whose movement was measured against an earlier position. aisFirstFixInZone counts vessels seen in the same window for the first time, which have nothing to compare against yet; they are in neither aisConcurrentInZone nor stranded.

aisGaps.countScope: count is a floor on hulls we stopped receiving, not a count of evasions. Read it against eligibleTankers, the screened tanker population, and against ambientDarkRate, the share of eligible non-tankers that went dark on the identical test. The tanker rate (36.6%) is running 1.7x the ambient rate (22.0%), a gap too large to read as ambient dropout alone.
aisGaps.vesselsTrackedScope: vesselsTracked is a cumulative, all-time, all-type total (every vessel ever recorded anywhere in the wider AIS bbox). It is not the screened population behind count: that population is tankers only, with 50 or more sightings, last seen inside the core area.

aisStaleFixNote: aisStaleFixInZone counts vessels still listed in the window whose last AIS fix is at least 60 minutes old and has not changed since the previous scrape. Their position is where they were, not where they are, so they are in none of aisConcurrentInZone, stranded or strandedOffshore. Of the stale vessels that reported again over three runs on 2026-09-26, 79 had not moved, 36 had moved and 15 had dropped off the feed, so the count left out is part held and part gone. Treat stranded and strandedOffshore as counts of vessels seen holding position within the last hour.

capeSnapshot.note: transitsLast24h counts port arrivals only (departures are not published upstream), across ports on both sides of the strait. Not a Hormuz crossing count. Use transits.count for that. An arrival is a port-area entry event rather than a distinct hull: adjacent ports double count and an anchorage reposition can re-trigger one, so read arrivals24hTotal as an activity index. expectedTotal is a 30-day forward book (ships expected within the next 30 days), not a queue waiting now. This feed is retired: the upstream port pages moved these aggregates behind a subscription on 2026-08-28 and have published none since, so the figures are frozen at asOf. For live Hormuz-corridor port activity use /api/v1/ports; for live Cape traffic use the cape row in chokepoints above.

carrierSuspensions.notes: Mediterranean Shipping Company routes Asia–Europe services via the Cape of Good Hope. Its March advisory suspended Middle East bookings and told ships in the area to shelter; it has published no vessel count since.

Maersk has suspended bookings to Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Saudi Gulf ports, Jordan and most UAE ports. It discharges at Fujairah and Khor Fakkan, outside the strait, and moves cargo overland to Jebel Ali, and it charges USD 1,000 a container on any vessel that transits the Strait of Hormuz. It said on 25 June that three of its vessels remained in the Gulf.

CMA CGM has activated Cape of Good Hope routing for all Asia–Europe services. Its chief financial officer said on the second-quarter earnings call on 30 July that eight of its vessels were inside the Gulf and unable to exit through the strait.
carrierSuspensions.sourceName: CMA CGM Q2 earnings call, via WorldCargo News

carrierSuspensions.notes: COSCO Shipping has suspended bookings to Bandar Abbas and routes Europe-bound services via the Cape. Two of its container ships crossed the strait in late March with Iranian clearance; it has not published a Gulf posture or vessel count since.
Hapag-Lloyd has suspended Hormuz transits and reroutes via the Cape. By 1 July it had moved all four of its vessels out of the Gulf.
Ocean Network Express suspended new bookings to and from the Persian Gulf on 2 March 2026, citing safety for crew, vessels and cargo. No advisory newer than that has been found.

chokepointsNote: preCrisisBaselineMedian on every row is computed over one fixed window (baselineWindowStart to baselineWindowEnd) anchored to the Hormuz crisis. For hormuz that window is a genuine pre-crisis baseline. For bab-el-mandeb, suez and cape it is not: those routes were already carrying diverted Red Sea traffic within that window, so preCrisisBaselineMedian for those rows reads as wartime volume, not a peacetime figure. baselineMedian is a different figure: the median of the latest 30 daily counts (trailing 30 days), not the fixed window.

bullets: TradeWinds News and L'Orient Today report several ships were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz as Iran launched fresh strikes.
Iran is reviewing the US ceasefire counterproposal, per The National Desk, WXLV and KBOI, with Strait of Hormuz terms still unclear.
India Today reports Iraq is importing petrol via Syria's Baniyas port as the Hormuz closure bites.
dailyBrief.summary: The Strait of Hormuz remains the site of active hostilities, with TradeWinds News and L'Orient Today reporting that several ships were attacked as Iran launched fresh strikes. On the diplomatic front, The National Desk, WXLV and KBOI all carry reports that Iran is reviewing the US ceasefire counterproposal, with the terms governing the Strait of Hormuz still described as unclear; ibtimes.com notes Iran received the US counterproposal and that tankers were reportedly hit in the strait shortly after. No attacker has been formally identified in the UKMTO reporting. Brent stood at $103.83 as of 15:32 UTC, up 0.17% over the prior 24 hours. IMF PortWatch recorded 1 transit on 2026-09-27, against a pre-crisis baseline of 85 per day. India Today reports Iraq is now importing petrol via Syria's Baniyas port as the closure reshapes regional supply logistics. The site's event index logged 60 indexed events in the last 24 hours. As of 15:20 UTC, 213 AIS-visible vessels were holding position away from berth in the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf watch box, a count that leaves out ships within 25km of a working port. On the Hormuz Index, Crisis Pressure, the state composite, sits in the extreme band, flat over 24 hours, with its value set by physical transit deviation alone; the Escalation Forecast sits in the elevated band, flat over 24 hours, with the Brent-WTI forward spread as its top contributor.

dataHealthNote: dataHealth.events reflects producer health, not event recency, UNLESS no event has arrived for 12 hours, after which it falls back to the plain event-age gate, so a very quiet stretch beyond 12 hours can still read stale even with a healthy pipeline. Use dataHealth.events.verifiedAt for the newest event time.

narrative.summary: The Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed to commercial traffic since February 28, 2026. Iran re-declared it closed after the July ceasefire collapsed, and the war has spread to a second chokepoint, where Yemen's Houthis now hold the Yemeni side of the Bab el-Mandeb. US forces have destroyed Iranian tankers and Iran has fired missiles at US warships and bases, while merchant ships are still being hit: Iran says it struck and detained a Togo-flagged tanker on September 17 for crossing without its permission, and on the evening of September 28 a projectile hit the Kuwaiti supertanker Al Funtas in the strait, starting a fire its crew put out. Drones launched from Iraq shut Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, the largest route around the strait, on September 11; Reuters and Bloomberg report a low-rate restart on September 22 that Saudi Aramco has not confirmed. How much is moving is now contested: US Central Command says it has escorted more than a billion barrels out in two months and that volumes are at a six-month high, and a US official said about 60 ships crossed on September 24, while independent trackers and our own count still show traffic far below pre-war levels, with Reuters counting nine commodity vessels that day. On September 23 a seafarer was killed when projectiles hit the bulk carrier Cape Dao off Oman. After indirect talks through mediators at the UN General Assembly, foreign minister Abbas Araghchi set out a seven-day plan on September 25: the United States would release frozen assets, lift oil sanctions and end its blockade, fighting would stop, and Iran would reopen the strait on the seventh day. President Trump rejected it in public on September 26, and Iran says it won't soften its terms. Since then the Revolutionary Guard has claimed to seize a US underwater drone, which the US denies, and says it fired warning shots at 19 ships on routes it hasn't approved. NBC News, citing unnamed US officials, reported that eight US Marines were hurt, none seriously, when an Iranian missile hit their ship in the strait on September 14, an attack not disclosed at the time. Iran now threatens to restrict every ship of any charterer that pushes vessels through without its approval. On September 30 the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said three more ships, among them a crude oil tanker and an LNG tanker, had been hit by unknown projectiles in the strait the day before, and Iran said it had received the US response to its plan and was reviewing it; the terms haven't been published.

pipelineBypass.name: Petroline (East-West Pipeline)
pipelineBypass.notes: Saudi Aramco's East-West Pipeline carries Arabian Light from Abqaiq to Yanbu on the Red Sea, the single largest non-Hormuz route for Gulf crude. Saudi Arabia shut it as a precaution on 11 September 2026 after drones launched from Iraq struck it in the Riyadh and Medina areas, damaging pipeline equipment. Reuters reported it had been carrying 4 to 5 million barrels a day, close to all of the Saudi crude rerouted away from the strait, though Kpler put its August flow nearer 2 million, the lowest since January. On 22 September Reuters and Bloomberg, citing industry sources, reported a restart at a low pumping rate. On 24 September Reuters reported crude moving through the line to Saudi refineries on the Red Sea coast, but tanker loadings at Yanbu had not resumed. Saudi Aramco and the energy ministry have not confirmed the restart or given a flow figure, and no export cargo has been confirmed, so this row stays offline until loadings resume or a flow figure is confirmed.
pipelineBypass.sourceName: EIA · World Oil Transit Chokepoints, Al Jazeera, CNN, Reuters via Zawya (24 Sep 2026), Kpler via Al Jazeera (14 Sep 2026)

pipelineBypass.name: ADCOP (Habshan-Fujairah)
pipelineBypass.notes: ADNOC's Habshan-Fujairah pipeline lifts UAE crude past the Strait of Hormuz to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman, where it loads on tankers transiting the open Indian Ocean.

pipelineBypass.name: Goreh-Jask Pipeline
pipelineBypass.notes: Iran's pipeline from the southwest oilfields to Jask on the Gulf of Oman bypasses the Strait, but throughput remains a fraction of nameplate capacity.

premium.note: Machine-payable premium endpoints (x402, USDC on Base): full vessel manifest with sanctions cross-reference, hourly history capped at one year with actual depth growing daily, one-call snapshot, structured daily brief, single-vessel dossiers, bulk export, real-time streaming, threshold-alert webhooks, a Hormuz flag rollup, a shadow-fleet risk screen of the vessels active on AIS in the Persian Gulf window, bunker and marine-fuel prices, and a modeled war-risk premium nowcast. $0.01-$0.50 per request, no key or account. MCP connector at the mcp URL.

strandedNote: `stranded` counts vessels seen holding position within the last hour, including ones at berth working cargo at regional ports such as Dubai and Abu Dhabi; a vessel with a stale AIS fix is left out and counted in aisStaleFixInZone instead, not folded into stranded. `strandedOffshore` excludes vessels within 25km of a working port and is the narrower figure the site's own narrative uses.

transits.cadenceNote: Completed daily transits (IMF PortWatch crossing count). Not the same as aisConcurrentInZone, which is a snapshot of vessels moving inside the wider Persian Gulf watch box right now, not the Strait channel itself.
transits.freshestDayNote: The newest PortWatch row is always a Sunday, because IMF publishes weekly on Tuesday against data carrying a ~2-day lag. Sunday is the lowest-traffic weekday in this series, so the freshest print reads low against the day before it even in a normal week. Compare it with earlier Sundays, or with baselineMedian, rather than with previousNTotal.

verdict.long: War-risk insurance has priced commercial transit through the Strait of Hormuz beyond the reach of most operators.
